text: Rachel Karen Green is a fictional character from the American sitcom Friends, one of the six main characters who appeared in all 236 episodes from the show's premiere on September 22, 1994, to its finale on May 6, 2004. Created by David Crane and Marta Kauffman, she is portrayed by Jennifer Aniston, who originally auditioned for the role after turning down a position as a cast member on Saturday Night Live. The role was initially offered to Téa Leoni, who declined to star in The Naked Truth, and Courteney Cox, who chose to play Monica Geller; Aniston, at the time a relatively unknown actress with prior experience in five short-lived sitcoms, was cast after the producers had already begun auditioning other actresses, including Elizabeth Berkley, Denise Richards, Melissa Rivers, Nicollette Sheridan, Parker Posey, Tiffani Thiessen, and Jami Gertz. Although Aniston was simultaneously starring in the CBS sitcom Muddling Through, which was ultimately canceled after only three months and 10 episodes—two weeks before Friends premiered—this allowed her to remain on the show. The character was originally named Rachel Robbins in the pilot and was conceived as a young woman unprepared for adulthood, relying on her parents’ wealth and initially described as spoiled and unskilled, with a personality that is "spoiled yet courageous" and "equipped to do nothing." Introduced in the pilot as a runaway bride who leaves her fiancé Barry Farber at the altar and moves in with her childhood friend Monica Geller, Rachel begins working as a waitress at Central Perk. Her relationship with Monica’s brother Ross Geller, whom she meets during her move to New York, becomes central to the series, beginning with Ross expressing his love for her at the end of the first season, despite her initially not knowing. Their on-again, off-again relationship spans the entire series, including Ross choosing Rachel over his girlfriend, their breakup during a "break," Ross marrying Emily (Helen Baxendale) after accidentally saying Rachel’s name in vows, divorcing Emily when she demands he stop being friends with Rachel, drunkenly marrying in Las Vegas during season five, and later co-parenting their daughter Emma, born in season eight from a one-night stand. Rachel briefly dates Joey Tribbiani in season nine, ending the relationship in season ten after realizing they are better as friends. Despite receiving a job offer in France, she decides to stay in New York and rekindle her relationship with Ross in the series finale, de-boarding her flight at the last minute. By the end of the series, Rachel has evolved from a dependent, spoiled "daddy's girl" into a successful businesswoman and self-assured woman. The character's second season haircut, known as the "Rachel," became an international phenomenon and remains one of the most popular hairstyles in history, despite Aniston personally disliking it. Rachel is regarded as a style icon due to her influence on 1990s womenswear, and her relationship with Ross is widely considered one of television’s most beloved. Critical reception has consistently praised Rachel, with The A.V. Club citing her as a major factor in the show’s early success. Aniston won an Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series and a Golden Globe Award for Best Performance by an Actress in a Television Series – Comedy or Musical, and her performance is credited with launching her successful film career and making her the show’s most famous cast member. The writers initially intended for Joey and Monica to be the show’s defining couple, but after seeing Aniston and David Schwimmer’s on-screen chemistry, they decided to focus on Ross and Rachel, creating a long-running "will they or won't they" dynamic that became a hallmark of the series. The first-season finale "The One Where Rachel Finds Out" marked a turning point, as Rachel learns of Ross’s true feelings and reciprocates, ending the "he’s pining, she’s oblivious" pattern. Their first kiss in season two’s "The One Where Ross Finds Out" was met with enthusiastic audience applause. Despite challenges, including Schwimmer’s initial objection to Ross divorcing Rachel, the writers ultimately decided to end the series with Ross and Rachel together, fulfilling audience expectations after ten years of anticipation. Post-series material, such as the spin-off Joey, suggests they eventually remarry. Rachel is the youngest of the six main characters and was raised in Long Island, New York. The ensemble format of Friends, which emphasized equal importance for all characters, was a key creative decision by Crane and Kauffman, and the cast became the first in television history to negotiate as a group for equal salaries, eventually earning $1 million per episode by seasons nine and ten. Aniston, who became the highest-paid television actress of all time alongside Cox and Lisa Kudrow, was initially hesitant to return for the final season but agreed after considering her own career and the show’s popularity. The character’s popularity has led to her being named one of the greatest television characters of all time.

Rachel Green, one of the six main characters of Friends, was raised in Long Island, New York, and is frequently described as spoiled, especially in her early appearances. Encyclopædia Britannica characterizes her as spoiled and funny, while her original pilot description by Crane and Kauffman portrays her as a spoiled yet courageous young woman who "has worked for none of what she has," unlike best friend Monica, and is initially "equipped to do nothing." James Endrst of the Hartford Courant labeled her "a spoiled rich kid," and the Daily News called her an "endearingly spoiled Daddy's girl." Kim Etingoff noted she is "spunky and sometimes spoiled," and TV Land described her as "naive." The Guardian's Ryan Gilbey observed that Rachel is neither insulated by self-regard like Monica nor swaddled in gormlessness like Phoebe. Frequently seen as fitting the "girl next door" archetype, Anne Bilson described her as "funny but not too funny, pretty but not too pretty, sexy but not too sexy, scatterbrained but not too scatterbrained," while Dominic Wills of TalkTalk called her "smart but ditzy, determined but undisciplined." Liat Kornowski of The Huffington Post described her as "beautiful, coveted, slightly neurotic, borderline egocentric." Jonathan Bernstein of The Daily Telegraph identified Rachel as "the self-absorbed one who goes from riches to rags," and Reign Magazine described her as "a human being full of vulnerability, humor and strength while aesthetically donning an undeniable beauty and allure." Originally unprepared for adult life, Rachel's personality evolved over time to become more self-sufficient and sympathetic, with Murray Pomerance noting that the growing boundary between Jennifer Aniston and Rachel made Aniston more authentic, and that both share normalcy, relatability, and expressiveness through hand gestures. Madeline Dimaggio wrote that Rachel struggled with being the spoiled, image-conscious "Daddy's girl" who fled from her wedding in the pilot, while BuddyTV stated she remains the most image-centric among the six, and Vogue's Edward Barsamian noted she was the most stylish and unabashedly fashion-obsessed character. TV Land summarized her as a "born shopper" who is "not necessarily a born worker," having never worked before moving in with Monica, but who is smart, resourceful, and chic, with a bright future. Splitsider's Mike D'Avria found Rachel had the third most sexual partners (14) and the highest percentage of serious monogamous relationships (71%), noting she continually meets men she wants to impress, and that her flirtations typically fail but result in serious relationships. Rachel is also the only female character to admit to having had a homosexual experience, alongside Chandler's admission of kissing a man in season 7, episode 4. In an interview with the Jewish Telegraph, Kauffman confirmed Rachel is Jewish, explaining that the name "Rachel Green" inherently implies Jewish identity. Vulture's Lindsey Weber noted similarities to Jewish culture, including referring to her grandmother as "Bubbe," Long Island origin, and engagement to a Jewish doctor. Stacy Wolf identified Rachel as embodying Jewish stereotypes in the 1990s, often serving as "the butt of the shows' jokes," and JDate's Rebecca Frankel cited her as one of the earliest and most prominent examples of the Jewish American Princess stereotype. Alicia R. Korenman described Rachel as spoiled, dependent on her father's and fiancé's money, horrified at the thought of working, inept in her attempts, and eventually overcoming a nose job. Evan Cooper described Rachel as a "de-semitized" Jew due to the absence of Jewish cultural experiences, Yiddish, or family members with Jewish surnames, noting she is more aligned with the "little woman" stereotype, while Robert Rorke labeled her a "rehabilitated Jewish American Princess," contrasting her with Amy (Christina Applegate), who remains selfish and narcissistic. Critical response to Rachel remained mostly positive throughout the show's ten-season run. John Reid of The A.V. Club credited Rachel with the pilot's success, calling her "the perfect stranger for this plot" and stating her arrival was a catalyst for the other characters' growth, as she is interested in finding meaning in life. Sonia Saraiya praised Rachel's first awkward encounter with Ross for displaying empathy and hailed her as a model for women coming of age in the 1990s—popular, pretty, dissatisfied with illusions, yet unwilling to embrace aggressive feminism. Joseph Hanania of The New York Times found Rachel's phone conversation with her father humorous, and Bob Shayne of the Los Angeles Times joked that his feelings for Rachel mirrored those of Gunther. Cosmopolitan called her "the best fictional gal pal we've ever had," People called her "spoiled-but-lovable," and TV Guide described her as "neurotic and adorable." Ellen Kerry of Heat hailed Rachel's transformation from waitress to businesswoman as "the best thing on tv." USA Today's Robert Bianco credited Rachel's pregnancy storyline with saving the show, noting it increased ratings and reversed decline, concluding that without it, Friends likely would have ended sooner. BDCwire ranked five episodes as Rachel's strongest: "The One with the Ball," "The One with Rachel's Inadvertent Kiss," "The One With The Football," "The One with the Fake Party," and "The One In Vegas, Part One." TVLine criticized Rachel for sleeping with ex-fiancé Barry in season one's "The One With the Evil Orthodontist" and for her role in season four's "The One With The Fake Party." The second-season episode "The One Where Dr. Ramoray Dies" generated mild controversy when Rachel and Monica argued over the last condom, with Rachel winning via rock-paper-scissors. Fans often criticized Aniston for Rachel's decisions. Within the first two seasons, Rachel became extremely popular among women, and her success remained a fan favorite throughout all ten seasons. Dominic Wills of TalkTalk noted that while Rachel was the general favorite, no one had a bad word to say about Jennifer Aniston, whose performance audiences instantly fell in love. Ken Tucker of Entertainment Weekly praised Aniston's portrayal of Rachel as having "prickly intelligence," David Zurawik of The Baltimore Sun cited her among the show's "very strong cast," and Tony Scott of Variety noted the principals displayed sharp sitcom skills. Robert Bianco of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette praised the female cast equally, TV Guide wrote that Aniston "instantly charmed audiences with her perfect looks and endearingly flawed persona," and Kevin Fallon of The Daily Beast described her tenure as not a "leading lady performance" but "the work of a brilliant character actress." Ryan Gilbey of The Guardian highlighted Aniston as the cast member "least reliant on goofball caricature," noting she was the only character a sane viewer might reasonably identify with. Andrew Collins of Radio Times called her a "natural comic performer, as adept with a subtle nose wrinkle as a full-on pratfall, and fluent in quick-fire patter." In 2002, Aniston won the Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series, and in 2003, she won the Golden Globe Award for Best Performance by an Actress in a Television Series – Comedy or Musical. Dominic Wills believes these awards were due to her "brilliant comic performances." Rachel has had several romantic relationships, most notably her on-again, off-again relationship with Ross. Though popular, the couple received mixed reviews; Katherine Hassel of the Daily Express called their relationship "the heart of the show," China Daily cited their reunion in the finale as a highlight, and Gary Susman of Rolling Stone believed audiences would not have been happy without their reunion. Joe Reid of The Wire considered the second season the only time Ross/Rachel was truly great, while Virgin Media stated their dynamics became "mightily tedious" by season ten. E! ranked them ninth among the greatest Friends couples, noting their relationship provided "enough iconic quotes to fill a book," with Phoebe's line "See? [Ross is] her lobster!" being among the most iconic. The season three breakup sparked debate over fault—Rachel for suggesting a break or Ross for sleeping with another woman afterward—leading E!'s Jenna Mullins to rule in Rachel's favor, stating Ross "blew it." The Jewish community welcomed the presence of a Jewish-American couple on prime time television, described by Lilith magazine as a "televisual first." Rachel and Ross are considered among television's greatest and most beloved couples, with Ninemsn calling them "everyone's favourite on ... off ... on (a break!) duo," Us Weekly and BuzzFeed ranking them first and second best television couples, respectively, and TV Guide placing them third as "the most iconic TV couple in recent memory." Extra ranked them eighth, writing "Never did we want two people to get together more than Ross ... and Rachel," and Refinery29 included them in a list of couples fans want to be together forever. They are often ranked among television's greatest "will they or won't they" couples, with Network Ten and Suggest naming them the greatest such couple, and Sarah Doran of Radio Times noting they became synonymous with the phrase "we're on a break." Phoebe's line has become one of the show's most popular and quoted. Kaitlin Reilly of Bustle defined the term as "the person of whom another is meant to be with forever," and Tara Aquino of Complex stated that "Every other person can tell you what exactly a 'Ross and Rachel' relationship means." Rachel's season eight pregnancy arc is credited with reviving the show's ratings and reviews. During season ten, Rachel's brief romance with Joey drew strong criticism from critics and fans, with Joshua Kurp of Splitsider attributing the show's final two seasons' performance to the Rachel/Joey/Ross love triangle, and Eric Goldman of IGN calling the storyline "questionable." Entertainment Tonight Canada ranked "The One After Rachel and Joey Kiss" among the show's ten worst episodes at number five, with I. P. Johnson calling it "desperate" and concluding "Jeers for even conceiving this romantic plot; cheers for abandoning it." E! enjoyed the Rachel and Joey relationship for bringing out positive aspects and shared humor, though Jenna Mullins of E! argued it was too late in the series, felt forced, and didn't make sense. After their breakup, there were many hints they would reunite, especially in seasons 8–10. In the final season, Rachel wants to sleep with Ross when her father has a heart attack, seeking "sympathy sex," which he declines. However, they sleep together the night before she leaves for Paris, leading Ross to admit he still loves her and wants to get back together. Rachel turns down the Paris job to be with Ross, realizing she still loves him, and the two agree "this is it," getting back together for good. Jennifer Aniston, who played Rachel, confirmed that after the series finale, Ross and Rachel got remarried, happily, and had at least one more child. Rachel's popularity established her as the show's breakout character; she is often ranked among the greatest characters in television history. Us Weekly ranked her the most beloved television character of the past two decades, citing her as "one of TV's most endearing personalities," Entertainment Weekly ranked her sixth on a similar list, and AOL TV included her among television's hundred "Greatest Women" at number 23, with author Kim Potts observing that Rachel grew from a one-note character into a more independent, caring pal.

Rachel, portrayed by Jennifer Aniston, becomes the show's breakout character and is widely recognized as one of the greatest television characters of all time, frequently ranked among the most beloved and influential female characters in TV history. Us Weekly named her the most beloved television character of the past two decades, while Entertainment Weekly ranked her sixth on a similar list, and AOL TV placed her at number 23 among television's hundred greatest women, noting her growth from a one-note character into an independent and caring friend. BuddyTV ranked her 15th as the funniest female sitcom character, and ChaCha listed her, Monica, and Phoebe at 11th, 12th, and 13th on their "Top 16 Female TV Characters of All Time." The Hollywood Reporter named her the 29th best female character in 2016, and Harper's Bazaar ranked her third most influential female TV character who changed the landscape of television, citing her promotion of female independence, open discussions about sex and pleasure, and her role in educating men on respectful treatment of women. Georgina Littlejohn of Entertainmentwise noted that Rachel inspired the character Penny from The Big Bang Theory, both being blonde, cute, funny, and likeable "girls-next-door." The name "Rachel" is commonly associated with baby names due to the character's popularity. Both Rachel and Aniston became fashion icons in the 1990s, especially among British women, with Vogue's Edward Barsamian crediting Rachel with inspiring "the cool New York look," and Stylist noting her revival of denim shirts and dungarees. Mahogany Clayton of StyleBlazer praised her for dominating fashion trends in stylish ways, while Heat magazine called her the "Fash Queen" for her influence on plaid skirts, denim, and overalls. BuzzFeed identified the mullet dress as a trend popularized by Rachel in the first season, and TV Guide published a list of "The 17 Ways Rachel from Friends Changed '90s Fashion." Rachel is often considered one of television's best-dressed characters, appearing on Elle's "50 Best Dressed Women on TV" list and PopSugar's list of "50 TV Shows That Changed the Way We Dress," where Friends was ranked 15th. InStyle ranked Friends 36th as the most fashionable TV show, praising the costumes of Rachel, Monica, and Phoebe. StyleCaster placed Rachel at number 28 among "The 50 Most Stylish TV Characters Of All Time," and Cosmopolitan compiled a list of 16 work outfits Rachel wore that are still wearable today. Virgin Media ranked her among television's sexiest, and Brides included her wedding dress in "The Best TV Wedding Dresses," commending its role in setting the tone for their decade-long relationship. Aniston, as the show's breakout star, became one of the most popular television actresses of her era, with USA Today dubbing her "our favorite Friend" and Kim Etingoff noting her fame "outshone" that of her co-stars, making her the first cast member to rise to prominence and the one with the most post-Friends success. Her performance in Friends launched her successful film career, with The Inquisitr News stating that Rachel "launched [Aniston's] success" and Splitsider asserting that she likely wouldn't have become a major movie star without Friends. Complex magazine ranked her the most attractive sitcom star of the 1990s, attributing her rise to her haircut, TV fame, and comedic talent, replacing Courteney Cox as the show's "established hottie." Steve Charnock of Yahoo! Movies noted that Aniston is the only main cast member to become a bona fide movie star since the show ended. Critics argue that many of her film roles are variations of Rachel, with Ryan Gilbey of The Guardian and Andrew Collins of Radio Times noting that she is "trapped" playing Rachel-like roles, and TV Guide stating she is usually cast as a variation of her neurotic and adorable Friends character. Aniston cites Rachel as one of three roles she is most grateful for and admits that being typecast has challenged her, as audiences struggle to move past the "Rachel" tag. The hairstyle known as the "Rachel," named after the character, is a bouncy layered shag inspired by Aniston's hair during the first and second seasons of Friends (1994–1996), debuting in the 20th episode, "The One with the Evil Orthodontist." Aniston believes her stylist, Chris McMillan, created it while under the influence of marijuana. The hairstyle became an international trend, with Marie Claire estimating 11 million women adopting it during the decade, and the Daily Express noting its popularity among British women, who visited salons with magazine pictures of Aniston asking for the look. Vanity Fair credited the hairstyle's popularity in the show's first year as cementing Friends' influence on style. The "Rachel" remains one of the most popular and iconic hairstyles in history, becoming the most popular in the U.S. since Farrah Fawcett's, and is frequently ranked among the greatest hairstyles of all time, with Redbook placing it fourth and Time ninth. The Huffington Post named it one of "The Most Famous TV Hairstyles Of All Time," US Weekly ranked it 17th most iconic, Glamour ranked it fourth on their "100 Best Hairstyles of All Time" and called it the most memorable hairstyle in television history, while The Sydney Morning Herald ranked it second greatest television hairstyle and Metro ranked it as the character's second-best hairstyle. It was also ranked sixth on Entertainment Weekly's list of "25 Fashion Moments That Changed Entertainment" and declared the most "desired" hairstyle of the Clinton era. Self's Zahra Barnes joked that Rachel's hair was the "true star of the show," and Elle's Sarah Carrillo believed the hairstyle helped make Friends a cultural phenomenon. Tom Jicha of The Baltimore Sun noted that the hairstyle was the show's only major cultural trend, while Complex's Josh Robertson and Glamour's Hannah Lyons Powell credited it as making Aniston the definitive hair icon of the '90s and the owner of arguably the most infamous and influential hairstyle of all time. Jim Vorel of Paste called it "the definition of influence," and Rebecca Cox of Glamour expressed gratitude that it remained a 1990s trend. In the second-season episode "The One with the Lesbian Wedding," Rachel jokes about her mother trying to reinvent her life by copying her haircut. Despite her association with the style, Aniston disliked it, finding it difficult to maintain without McMillan, stating she would curse him every time she blow-dried it, that it required three brushes like "doing surgery," and that she would rather shave her head than wear it for life. Since Aniston, numerous celebrities have worn variations of the "Rachel," including Cameron Diaz, Rachel McAdams, Emma Watson, Reese Witherspoon, Julia Roberts, Tina Fey, Tyra Banks, and Lily Allen.
